title: Seeing the state in action: Public preferences about and judgments of common police–civilian interactions
rationale: The experiments present written police–civilian vignettes with independently randomized attributes and, in the main experiments, a later randomized account of the interaction outcome. This is a survey-content experiment; its factorial text assembly and sequential outcome measurements require original questionnaire inspection before parser compatibility can be established.

title: LLM-generated messages can persuade humans on policy issues
rationale: Participants are randomized to written policy messages and report pre/post policy support. The experiments include pools of message exemplars within conditions, human-curated messages, and multiple policy topics. This is a survey-content experiment; the original instrument and stimulus-to-response mapping are needed to assess the parser.

title: Men’s Overpersistence and the Gender Gap in Science and Mathematics
rationale: Study 1 randomizes mathematical-task difficulty and repeatedly lets participants choose problems, answer them, and receive correctness/payment feedback. Study 3 gives all participants the same hard-math/easy-verbal task and measures correlates through questionnaires; Study 2 is observational. These are task and observational designs rather than the project’s intended randomized survey-content experiment. The interactive task is outside the simple text-treatment parser; candidate article counts remain unchanged.

title: Differences in misinformation sharing can lead to politically asymmetric sanctions
rationale: The article includes previously collected survey conditions that ask participants to rate accuracy or sharing intentions for headlines, alongside new and reused observational social-media data. Experimental-data provenance and the original instruments require inspection; this article should not be interpreted as a separate newly fielded experimental dataset.

title: Psychological Underpinnings of Partisan Bias in Tie Formation on Social Media
rationale: The survey component randomizes one of three fixed mock-account biographies and asks hypothetical follow-back intentions and explanations. It appears compatible as a fixed survey experiment; the separate live Twitter field experiment would require a different data structure.

title: How and when candidate race affects inferences about ideology and group favoritism
rationale: The first experiment shows one independently randomized multi-attribute candidate profile; the second shows five profiles with constrained race randomization and randomized district characteristics. This complex profile construction exceeds the targeted simple fixed-arm parser structure, even though the responses are ratings rather than paired choices.
